exercises.questionText: Two letters are to be chosen from A, B and C, where order is important. List all the different ways that this may be done.

solution.formula: Systematic listing: fix the first letter, then list every possible second letter (no letter used twice).
steps: Given: letters A, B, C; choose 2, order matters, no repeats. Goal: list every arrangement.
First letter A: second letter B or C $\Rightarrow$ AB, AC
First letter B: second letter A or C $\Rightarrow$ BA, BC
First letter C: second letter A or B $\Rightarrow$ CA, CB
solution.finalAnswer: AB, AC, BA, BC, CA, CB (6 arrangements)
solution.tip: Because order matters, AB and BA are different arrangements, so list both.

exercises.questionText: Two letters are to be chosen from A, B and C, where order is important. Use the multiplication principle to calculate the number of ways that this may be done.

solution.formula: Multiplication principle: if one choice can be made in $m$ ways and the next in $n$ ways, together they can be made in $m \times n$ ways.
steps: Given: 3 letters, 2 positions, no repeats. Goal: number of ordered selections.
Second position: one letter has been used, so 2 choices.
solution.tip: Check against your list in part (a): both methods must give 6.

exercises.questionText: Two letters are to be chosen from A, B and C, where order is important (no repeats). Determine the probability that the last letter will be a B.

steps: Given: sample space $\xi = \{AB, AC, BA, BC, CA, CB\}$, so $n(\xi) = 6$. Goal: $\Pr(\text{last letter is B})$.
Outcomes ending in B: AB, CB, so $n(E) = 2$.
solution.tip: Always simplify the fraction: $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$.

exercises.questionText: Two letters are to be chosen from A, B and C, where order is important. Use the multiplication principle to calculate the number of ways the two letters can be chosen if the first letter is replaced after selection.

solution.formula: Multiplication principle with replacement: $n \times n$ choices for 2 positions.
steps: Given: 3 letters, 2 positions, the first letter is replaced so repeats are allowed. Goal: number of ways.
Second position: still 3 choices (the letter was replaced).
solution.finalAnswer: There are $9$ ways (AA, AB, AC, BA, BB, BC, CA, CB, CC).
solution.tip: With replacement, the number of choices does not drop for the second pick.

exercises.questionText: List all the different arrangements possible for a group of 2 colours to be chosen from B (blue), G (green), Y (yellow) and R (red).

solution.formula: Systematic listing; check with the multiplication principle ${}^{4}P_{2} = 4 \times 3 = 12$.
steps: Given: 4 colours, choose 2, order matters, no repeats. Goal: list all arrangements.
Start with B: BG, BY, BR
Start with G: GB, GY, GR
Start with Y: YB, YG, YR
Start with R: RB, RG, RY
solution.finalAnswer: BG, BY, BR, GB, GY, GR, YB, YG, YR, RB, RG, RY (12 arrangements)
solution.tip: Work through the first colour in a fixed order so you do not miss or repeat any arrangement.

exercises.questionText: List all the different arrangements possible for a group of 3 letters to be chosen from A, B and C.

steps: Given: 3 letters, all 3 used, order matters. Goal: list all arrangements.
solution.finalAnswer: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA (6 arrangements)
solution.tip: Arranging all $n$ distinct objects always gives $n!$ arrangements.

exercises.questionText: Use the multiplication principle to calculate how many ways an arrangement of 2 letters can be chosen from A, B, C, D, E, F and G.

steps: Given: 7 different letters, 2 positions, no repeats. Goal: number of arrangements.
solution.tip: Reduce the number of choices by one for each position already filled.

exercises.questionText: Calculate how many ways an arrangement of 3 letters can be chosen from 7 different letters.

steps: Given: 7 different letters, 3 positions, no repeats. Goal: number of arrangements.
solution.tip: Write one factor per position: 3 positions means 3 factors.

exercises.questionText: Calculate how many ways an arrangement of 4 letters can be chosen from 7 different letters.

steps: Given: 7 different letters, 4 positions, no repeats. Goal: number of arrangements.
solution.tip: You can reuse part (b): $210 \times 4 = 840$.

exercises.questionText: Calculate how many different arrangements of 5 letters can be made from 7 letters.

steps: Given: 7 different letters, 5 positions, no repeats. Goal: number of arrangements.
solution.tip: Stop multiplying once you have one factor for each of the 5 positions.

exercises.questionText: Arrangements of 5 letters are made from the 7 letters A, B, C, D, E, F and G. Determine how many possible arrangements there are beginning with an E.

solution.formula: Multiplication principle with a fixed first position.
steps: Given: 5-letter arrangements from 7 letters, first letter must be E. Goal: number of such arrangements.
1st position: must be E, so 1 choice.
solution.tip: Fill the restricted position first, then count the rest.

exercises.questionText: Determine the number of different subsets formed from a set with 3 elements.

solution.formula: Number of subsets of a set with $n$ elements $= 2^n$ (each element is either in or out).
steps: Each element has 2 options (in or out): $2 \times 2 \times 2$
solution.tip: Remember the empty set and the whole set both count as subsets.

exercises.questionText: Determine the number of different subsets formed from a set with 5 elements.

solution.tip: It is $2^n$, not $n^2$: $5^2 = 25$ is wrong.

exercises.questionText: Determine the number of different subsets formed from a set with 9 elements.

solution.tip: Each extra element doubles the number of subsets.

exercises.questionText: Recall the definition of $n!$ and write $4!$ in expanded form.

solution.tip: Count down from $n$ all the way to 1.

exercises.questionText: Recall the definition of $n!$ and write $5!$ in expanded form.

solution.tip: Note $5! = 5 \times 4!$.

exercises.questionText: Recall the definition of $n!$ and write $6!$ in expanded form.

solution.tip: There should be exactly 6 factors in $6!$.

exercises.questionText: Recall the definition of $n!$ and write $7!$ in expanded form.

solution.tip: Factorials grow very quickly; $7!$ is already 5040.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $\dfrac{9!}{5!}$ without using a calculator.

solution.formula: Cancel common factors: $\dfrac{n!}{r!} = n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times (r+1)$ for $r < n$.
solution.tip: Do not divide 9 by 5; cancel the whole $5!$ instead.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $\dfrac{10!}{4!}$ without using a calculator.

solution.tip: Pair factors (e.g. $10 \times 9$, $8 \times 7$, $6 \times 5$) to make mental arithmetic easier.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $\dfrac{7!}{3!}$ without using a calculator.

solution.tip: $\frac{7!}{3!}$ is not $\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)!$.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $\dfrac{6!}{0!}$ without using a calculator.

solution.tip: $0! = 1$, not 0, so you are never dividing by zero here.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $10!$.

solution.tip: Use the $x!$ key on your calculator for large factorials.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $14!$.

solution.tip: Some calculators show this in scientific notation; write out all the digits.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $9!$.

solution.tip: Build up from a factorial you already know.

exercises.questionText: Evaluate $16!$.

solution.tip: If your calculator shows $2.09 \times 10^{13}$, that is a rounded value, not the exact answer.

exercises.questionText: Calculate ${}^{8}P_{2}$ by expressing it in expanded form.

solution.tip: ${}^{n}P_{r}$ always has exactly $r$ factors.

exercises.questionText: Calculate ${}^{7}P_{5}$ by expressing it in expanded form.

solution.tip: The last factor is $n - r + 1 = 7 - 5 + 1 = 3$.

exercises.questionText: Calculate ${}^{8}P_{7}$ by expressing it in expanded form.

solution.tip: Notice ${}^{8}P_{7} = 8!$ because the missing factor is just 1.

exercises.questionText: Write ${}^{9}P_{6}$ as a quotient of factorials and hence evaluate.

solution.tip: The bottom factorial is $(n-r)!$, not $r!$.

exercises.questionText: Write ${}^{5}P_{2}$ as a quotient of factorials and hence evaluate.

solution.tip: Check: $5 \times 4 = 20$.

exercises.questionText: Write ${}^{18}P_{5}$ as a quotient of factorials and hence evaluate.

solution.tip: Cancel before multiplying; $18!$ itself is far too large to work with by hand.

exercises.questionText: Use your calculator to determine the value of ${}^{20}P_{6}$.

solution.tip: On the calculator, enter 20, then nPr, then 6.

exercises.questionText: Use your calculator to determine the value of ${}^{800}P_{2}$.

solution.tip: Typing $800!$ will overflow a calculator; use nPr or just the two factors.

exercises.questionText: Use your calculator to determine the value of ${}^{18}P_{5}$.

solution.tip: Use the calculator result to check your hand calculation in Question 10(c).

exercises.questionText: Determine how many different arrangements of 5 counters can be made using 3 red and 2 blue counters.

steps: Given: $n = 5$ counters, 3 identical red, 2 identical blue. Goal: number of distinct arrangements.
solution.tip: Divide by the factorial of each group of identical objects, because swapping identical counters gives the same arrangement.

exercises.questionText: Determine how many different arrangements of 9 counters can be made using 4 black, 3 red and 2 blue counters.

steps: Given: $n = 9$; 4 black, 3 red, 2 blue. Goal: number of distinct arrangements.
solution.tip: Check the group sizes add to $n$: $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$.

exercises.questionText: Write ${}^{8}C_{3}$ as a statement in terms of permutations.

solution.tip: Dividing by $r!$ removes the different orders of the same group.

exercises.questionText: Write ${}^{19}C_{2}$ as a statement in terms of permutations.

solution.tip: The $r$ in $r!$ matches the subscript of $C$.

exercises.questionText: Write ${}^{1}C_{1}$ as a statement in terms of permutations.

solution.tip: Choosing all $n$ items can only be done in 1 way.

exercises.questionText: Write ${}^{5}C_{0}$ as a statement in terms of permutations.

solution.tip: There is exactly one way to choose nothing.

exercises.questionText: A teddy bear's wardrobe consists of 3 different hats, 4 different shirts and 2 different pairs of pants. Determine how many different outfits the teddy bear can wear.

steps: Given: 3 hats, 4 shirts, 2 pants; one of each per outfit. Goal: number of outfits.
solution.tip: Multiply (not add) when one choice is made from each category.

exercises.questionText: A surfboard is to have 1 colour on its top and a different colour on its bottom. The 3 possible colours are red, blue and green. Calculate how many different ways the surfboard can be coloured.

steps: Given: 3 colours; top and bottom must differ. Goal: number of colourings.
solution.tip: Top red/bottom blue is different from top blue/bottom red, so order matters.

exercises.questionText: A new phone comes with a choice of 3 cases, 2 different-sized screens and 2 different storage capacities. With these choices, determine how many different arrangements are possible.

steps: Given: 3 cases, 2 screens, 2 storage options. Goal: number of phone set-ups.
solution.tip: One factor for each independent choice.

exercises.questionText: Messages can be sent by placing 3 different coloured flags in order on a pole. If the flags come in 4 colours, determine how many different messages can be sent.

steps: Given: 4 colours, 3 positions, colours all different, order matters. Goal: number of messages.
solution.tip: 'Different coloured flags' means no colour is repeated.

exercises.questionText: Hani and Mary's restaurant offers its patrons a choice of 4 entrees, 10 main courses and 5 desserts. Determine how many choices of 3-course meals (entree, main, dessert) are available.

steps: Given: 4 entrees, 10 mains, 5 desserts. Goal: number of 3-course meals.
solution.tip: Multiply the number of options for each course.

exercises.questionText: Hani and Mary's restaurant offers its patrons a choice of 4 entrees, 10 main courses and 5 desserts. Determine how many choices of entree and main course are offered.

steps: Given: 4 entrees, 10 mains. Goal: number of entree-main pairs.
solution.tip: Only include the courses that are part of the meal.

exercises.questionText: Hani and Mary's restaurant offers its patrons a choice of 4 entrees, 10 main courses and 5 desserts. Determine how many choices of meals comprising a main course and dessert are offered.

steps: Given: 10 mains, 5 desserts. Goal: number of main-dessert pairs.
solution.tip: Leave out the entree factor since no entree is chosen.

exercises.questionText: A soccer club will appoint a president and a vice-president. Eight people have volunteered for either of the two positions. Determine how many different ways these positions can be filled.

steps: Given: 8 people, 2 distinct positions, one person per position. Goal: number of ways.
solution.tip: The positions are different, so order matters and we use permutations.

exercises.questionText: A soccer club will appoint a president and a vice-president. For two years the same 8 people volunteered for these positions. Determine the probability that one of them is president for both years.

steps: Given: 8 candidates each year for president, chosen at random. Goal: $\Pr(\text{same person is president both years})$.
Same person both years: 8 outcomes (one for each person), so $n(E) = 8$.
solution.tip: Whoever is president in year 1, the chance they are chosen again in year 2 is $\frac{1}{8}$.

exercises.questionText: Determine how many different permutations can be made using the 11 letters of the word ABRACADABRA.

steps: Given: ABRACADABRA has 11 letters: A $\times 5$, B $\times 2$, R $\times 2$, C $\times 1$, D $\times 1$ (check: $5+2+2+1+1 = 11$).
solution.tip: Count every repeated letter carefully before dividing.

exercises.questionText: A collection of 12 books is to be arranged on a shelf. The books consist of 3 copies of Great Expectations, 5 copies of Catcher in the Rye and 4 copies of Huntin', Fishin' and Shootin'. Determine how many different arrangements of these books are possible.

steps: Given: 12 books; identical groups of 3, 5 and 4 (check: $3+5+4 = 12$). Goal: number of arrangements.
solution.tip: Copies of the same book are identical, so divide by each group's factorial.

exercises.questionText: Apply the concept of ${}^{n}C_{r}$ to calculate the number of ways three types of ice-cream can be chosen in any order from a supermarket freezer containing 3 types of ice-cream.

solution.tip: Choosing all of the items can only be done in one way.

exercises.questionText: Apply the concept of ${}^{n}C_{r}$ to calculate the number of ways three types of ice-cream can be chosen in any order from a supermarket freezer containing 6 types of ice-cream.

solution.tip: 'In any order' signals combinations, not permutations.

exercises.questionText: Apply the concept of ${}^{n}C_{r}$ to calculate the number of ways three types of ice-cream can be chosen in any order from a supermarket freezer containing 10 types of ice-cream.

solution.tip: Remember to divide by $3! = 6$.

exercises.questionText: Apply the concept of ${}^{n}C_{r}$ to calculate the number of ways three types of ice-cream can be chosen in any order from a supermarket freezer containing 12 types of ice-cream.

solution.tip: Without dividing by $3!$ you would get 1320, which counts each selection 6 times.

exercises.questionText: A mixed netball team must have 3 women and 4 men in the side. If the squad has 6 women and 5 men wanting to play, determine how many different teams are possible.

steps: Given: choose 3 of 6 women and 4 of 5 men; order not important. Goal: number of teams.
solution.tip: Multiply the separate selections; do not add them.

exercises.questionText: Jasmin has a phone that has a 4-digit security code. She remembers that the first number in the code was 9 and that the others were 3, 4 and 7 but forgets the order of the last 3 digits. Determine how many different trials she must make to be sure of unlocking the phone.

steps: Given: first digit fixed as 9; digits 3, 4, 7 fill the last 3 places in some order. Goal: number of possible codes.
solution.finalAnswer: She must make $6$ trials to be sure.
solution.tip: The fixed digit contributes a factor of 1.

exercises.questionText: Determine how many different 4-digit numbers can be made from the numbers 1, 3, 5 and 7 if the numbers can be repeated (that is 3355 and 7777 are valid).

steps: Given: 4 digits available, 4 places, repetition allowed. Goal: number of 4-digit numbers.
solution.tip: When repeats are allowed, the number of choices stays the same for every place.

exercises.questionText: There are 26 players in an online game. Determine how many different results for 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th can occur.

steps: Given: 26 players, 4 ranked places, order matters. Goal: number of results.
solution.tip: Placings are ordered, so use $P$, not $C$.

exercises.questionText: A rowing crew consists of 4 rowers who sit in a definite order. Determine how many different crews are possible if 5 people try out for selection.

steps: Given: 5 people, 4 ordered seats. Goal: number of crews.
solution.tip: 'Definite order' means the seat positions matter.

exercises.questionText: The school musical needs a producer, director, musical director and script coach. Nine people have volunteered for any of these positions. Determine how many different ways the positions can be filled. (Note: One person cannot take on more than 1 position.)

steps: Given: 9 people, 4 different positions, no one holds two. Goal: number of ways.
solution.tip: Distinct job titles make order important.

exercises.questionText: A shelf holding 24 cans of dog food is to be stacked using 9 cans of Yummy and 15 cans of Ruff for Dogs. Determine how many different ways the shelf can be stocked.

steps: Given: 24 cans; 9 identical Yummy and 15 identical Ruff for Dogs. Goal: number of arrangements.
$\dfrac{24!}{9!\,15!} = {}^{24}C_{9}$ (choose which 9 of the 24 places hold Yummy)
solution.tip: Use the nCr key: $24 \, \text{nCr} \, 9$.

exercises.questionText: A committee of 5 students is to be chosen from 6 boys and 8 girls. Use ${}^{n}C_{r}$ and the multiplication principle to calculate how many committees can be formed.

steps: Given: $6 + 8 = 14$ students, choose 5, order not important. Goal: number of committees.
solution.tip: With no gender condition, choose from the whole group of 14.

exercises.questionText: A committee of 5 students is to be chosen from 6 boys and 8 girls. Use ${}^{n}C_{r}$ and the multiplication principle to calculate how many of the committees contain exactly 2 boys and 3 girls.

steps: Given: choose 2 of 6 boys and 3 of 8 girls. Goal: number of committees.
solution.tip: Choose each group separately, then multiply.

exercises.questionText: Calculate the values of ${}^{12}C_{3}$ and ${}^{12}C_{9}$.

solution.tip: Cancel the larger factorial in the denominator to save work.

exercises.questionText: Calculate the values of ${}^{15}C_{8}$ and ${}^{15}C_{7}$.

solution.tip: Both have the denominator $7!\,8!$, so they must be equal.

exercises.questionText: Calculate the values of ${}^{10}C_{1}$ and ${}^{10}C_{9}$.

solution.tip: Choosing 9 to include is the same as choosing 1 to leave out.

exercises.questionText: Calculate the values of ${}^{8}C_{3}$ and ${}^{8}C_{5}$.

solution.tip: Notice $3 + 5 = 8$ again.

exercises.questionText: In part (a) you calculated ${}^{12}C_{3}$ and ${}^{12}C_{9}$, ${}^{15}C_{8}$ and ${}^{15}C_{7}$, ${}^{10}C_{1}$ and ${}^{10}C_{9}$, ${}^{8}C_{3}$ and ${}^{8}C_{5}$. Describe what you notice in your results. Give your answer as a general statement such as 'The value of ${}^{n}C_{r}$ is...'.

steps: Each pair gave equal values: 220 and 220, 6435 and 6435, 10 and 10, 56 and 56.
In each pair the two $r$ values add to $n$: $3 + 9 = 12$, $8 + 7 = 15$, $1 + 9 = 10$, $3 + 5 = 8$.
Reason: ${}^{n}C_{n-r} = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!} = {}^{n}C_{r}$; choosing $r$ items to take is the same as choosing $n - r$ items to leave behind.
solution.finalAnswer: The value of ${}^{n}C_{r}$ is the same as the value of ${}^{n}C_{n-r}$.

exercises.questionText: Lotto is a game played by choosing 6 numbers from 45. No number can be drawn more than once, and the order in which the numbers are selected does not matter. Calculate how many different selections of 6 numbers can be made from 45.

solution.tip: Order does not matter in Lotto, so use combinations.

exercises.questionText: Lotto is a game played by choosing 6 numbers from 45 (order does not matter, no repeats). Suppose the first numbers drawn at the official draw are 42, 3 and 18. Determine how many selections of 6 numbers will contain these 3 numbers.

steps: Given: 3 of the 6 numbers are fixed (42, 3, 18). Goal: number of selections containing all three.
The other 3 numbers are chosen from the remaining $45 - 3 = 42$ numbers.
solution.tip: Remove the fixed numbers from both the pool and the number still to be chosen.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. A ball is taken at random, its colour is noted, and it is then replaced before a second ball is chosen at random and its colour is noted. Show the possible outcomes with a fully labelled tree diagram.

solution.formula: Tree diagram; multiplication rule for independent events: $\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A) \times \Pr(B)$
steps: Given: 10 balls (7 R, 3 W), with replacement. $\Pr(R) = \dfrac{7}{10} = 0.7$, $\Pr(W) = \dfrac{3}{10} = 0.3$ on each draw.
From each first branch, second draw branches: R (0.7), W (0.3).
solution.finalAnswer: Tree: 1st draw R (0.7) / W (0.3); 2nd draw R (0.7) / W (0.3) from each. Outcomes RR 0.49, RW 0.21, WR 0.21, WW 0.09.
solution.tip: With replacement, the second-draw branch probabilities are the same as the first.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. A ball is taken at random, its colour is noted, and it is then replaced before a second ball is chosen. As the first ball was chosen, how many balls were in the bag?

solution.finalAnswer: There were $10$ balls in the bag.
solution.tip: Add both colours to get the total.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. A ball is taken at random, its colour is noted, and it is then replaced before a second ball is chosen. As the second ball was chosen, how many balls were in the bag?

solution.formula: With replacement the total is unchanged.
steps: The first ball was put back, so the bag again has $7 + 3 = 10$ balls.
solution.finalAnswer: There were $10$ balls in the bag.
solution.tip: 'Replaced' means the bag is back to its starting state.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. A ball is taken at random, its colour is noted, and it is then replaced before a second ball is chosen. Does the probability of choosing a red or white ball change from the first selection to the second? Explain.

solution.formula: Independent events: the first outcome does not affect the second.
steps: The ball is replaced, so the second selection is from the same 7 red and 3 white: $\Pr(R) = 0.7$, $\Pr(W) = 0.3$.
solution.finalAnswer: No. The ball is replaced, so the probabilities stay the same; the events are independent.
solution.tip: Replacement makes successive draws independent.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. A ball is taken at random, its colour is noted, and it is then replaced before a second ball is chosen. Calculate the probability of choosing a red ball twice.

solution.tip: Multiply along the branches of the tree.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. The process of choosing two balls is repeated, but this time the first selection is not replaced. As the second ball is chosen, how many balls are in the bag?

solution.formula: Without replacement the total drops by 1.
solution.finalAnswer: There are $9$ balls in the bag.
solution.tip: The first ball stays out, so the denominator becomes 9.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. Two balls are chosen and the first selection is not replaced. Does the probability of choosing a red or white ball change from the first selection to the second? Explain.

solution.formula: Dependent events: the first outcome changes the second.
steps: If the first is red, the bag has 6 R and 3 W: $\Pr(R) = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
If the first is white, the bag has 7 R and 2 W: $\Pr(R) = \dfrac{7}{9}$.
solution.finalAnswer: Yes. One ball has been removed from the bag, so the probabilities for the second draw depend on the first (dependent events).
solution.tip: Without replacement, both the count of that colour and the total change.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. Two balls are chosen and the first selection is not replaced. Construct a fully labelled tree diagram to show all possible outcomes.

solution.formula: Tree diagram; multiplication rule for dependent events: $\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A) \times \Pr(B \mid A)$
steps: After R (6 R, 3 W left): R $\dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.67$, W $\dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.33$.
After W (7 R, 2 W left): R $\dfrac{7}{9} \approx 0.78$, W $\dfrac{2}{9} \approx 0.22$.
solution.finalAnswer: Tree: 1st R (0.7) then R ($\frac{2}{3}$) / W ($\frac{1}{3}$); 1st W (0.3) then R ($\frac{7}{9}$) / W ($\frac{2}{9}$). Outcomes RR $\frac{7}{15}$, RW $\frac{7}{30}$, WR $\frac{7}{30}$, WW $\frac{1}{15}$.
solution.tip: Each pair of second-stage branches must still add to 1.

exercises.questionText: A bag contains 7 red and 3 white balls. Two balls are chosen and the first selection is not replaced. Calculate the probability of choosing two red balls.

solution.formula: Multiplication rule for dependent events: $\Pr(RR) = \Pr(R_1) \times \Pr(R_2 \mid R_1)$
solution.tip: Use exact fractions; multiplying rounded values ($0.7 \times 0.67 = 0.469$) gives a slightly wrong answer.

exercises.questionText: A combination lock has 3 digits, each from 0 to 9. Determine how many combinations are possible.

steps: Given: 3 dials, each with 10 digits (0 to 9), repeats allowed. Goal: number of combinations.
solution.tip: Digits can repeat on a lock, so each dial has all 10 choices.

exercises.questionText: A combination lock has 3 digits, each from 0 to 9. The lock mechanism becomes loose and will open if the digits are within 1 either side of the correct digit. For example, if the true combination is 382, then the lock will open on 271, 272, 371, 493 and so on. Determine how many combinations would unlock the safe.

steps: Given: each dial opens on the correct digit or 1 either side. Goal: number of opening combinations.
solution.tip: This assumes no correct digit is 0 or 9; at an end there may be fewer neighbours unless the dial wraps around.

exercises.questionText: A combination lock has 3 digits, each from 0 to 9. The lock mechanism becomes loose and will open if the digits are within 1 either side of the correct digit. List the possible combinations that would open the lock if the true combination is 382.

solution.formula: Systematic listing: first digit $\in \{2,3,4\}$, second $\in \{7,8,9\}$, third $\in \{1,2,3\}$
solution.tip: Vary the last digit fastest so the list stays organised.
